messages.subject: Re: [poppr] Reconfirmation of dendrogram tree results made by using POPPr package
messages.subject_clean: [poppr] Reconfirmation of dendrogram tree results made by using POPPr package
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm afraid I'm not sure what you are asking here, so I will try my best to give some general information.

First, since you have SNP data, you may wish to use the phangorn package with dist.hamming or dist.ml <http://dist.ml> or the ape package with dist.dna, but be sure to convert your heterozygous sites to ambiguous characters first. You can bootstrap these with the boot.phylo function.

----------

In general bootstrapping procedures need three things:

1. original data with variables (loci) in columns and samples in rows
2. a function to calculate distance
3. a function to calculate a tree from the distance

in aboot, these are the "x", "distance" and "tree" parameters.
in pvclust, these are the "data", "method.dist", and "method.hclust" parameters

The results of the bootstrapping procedure will tell you about the internal consistency of your data based on the chosen variables, but not necessarily how likely those groupings are.

----------

I'm not entirely sure what pvclust does, but it looks like it supplies a general method to bootstrap dendrograms similar to aboot, however there are important differences to be aware of:

The bootstrapping in pvclust appears to be based on generic distance methods for tabular data, aboot on the other hand, acts specifically on genind and genlight objects (which is necessary because alleles within a locus need to be resampled together).

Your code for pvclust appears to be passing a distance matrix in place of the original data, using a correlation coefficient for the distance method and "hclust" for the tree (which is the same as UPGMA).
This defeats the purpose of the bootstrapping procedure because you are no longer bootstrapping independent loci. Is there a specific reason why you want to use pvclust?

A minor note: your call to "aboot" uses Nei's distance, which was designed for populations, not individuals [1, 2]. Since you used the results of "bitwise.dist"* for pvclust, you may wish to use an equivalent distance for "aboot" if you wish to compare them.

[1]: https://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/10.1094/PHYTO-12-16-0425-RVW (box 3)
[2]: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/poppr/vignettes/algo.pdf (section 3.4)
* bitwise.dist was designed for genlight objects, specifically. Since you passed a genind object to it, it calls "prevosti.dist" internally.

I hope that helps,
Zhian

-----

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

> I used bitwise.dist method because this can handle       SNP data with missing values.

As I mentioned earlier, bitwise.dist is the equivalent of prevosti.dist. The only difference is that, if you have genlight data (which optimizes storage), then bitwise.dist will be able to handle it more efficiently.

> The reason behind using pvclust is I have ~ more than 1100 individuals and I cannot see their cluster allocation clearly on my screen and to extract      significant clusters, but this I can do in PVLCUST using pvpick.

Again, the way you were using pvclust will not give you useful information. Please do not use that package for these data. There are other packages that can draw rectangles around your data. If you convert your tree to an hclust object with as.hclust(), you can draw a rectangle around it using rect.hclust() OR you can use the dendextend package do achieve the same thing and more. Please read the documentation and explore the examples of functions like plot.phylo() to see what's possible.

>  Which distance method I can use in aboot for individuals?

Please read the resources I linked in the previous email. If you do not have access to Phytopathology, I can send you a copy of the article. In short, Prevosti's distance (a simple mismatch distance) will work just fine.

> Is it possible to extract significant clusters (>95%  significance level) in abbot       also?

Yes, but that depends on your definition of significance. Bootstrapping is more or less a "feel good" measure that shows the internal consistency of your data.

Hope that helps,
Zhian

Hi John,

I think we should stick to the Pinf dataset for this conversation. Part of the purpose of this forum is to document our attempts so that it not only helps you but it may provide help for someone in the future who may have a similar issue. Because the Pinf dataset is available with poppr it means that others will have access to it so it will provide a full example.

Based on the criteria you've provided, I think I got you almost all the way there. Lets repeat it with some changes.

library(poppr)
data("Pinf")
x <- tab(Pinf)

# Create some 'microvariants'
mv <- c(15, 23, 26, 36, 43, 45, 55, 105)
colnames(x)[mv] <- paste(colnames(x)[mv], "_2", sep="")

# Assume everything is one population
x <- colSums(x, na.rm = TRUE)
# Create a factor of loci names
loci <- as.factor(unlist(lapply(strsplit(names(x), split=".", fixed=TRUE), function(x){x[1]})))
# Create a list where each locus is an element
x <- split(x, loci)
# Convert to percentage

x <- lapply(x, function(x){x/sum(x)})
# Rename the alleles so they will be numeric as in the post
x <- lapply(x, function(x){names(x) <- unlist(lapply(strsplit(names(x), split='.', fixed=TRUE), function(x){x[2]})); x})
# Handle 'microvariants'
x <- lapply(x, function(x){names(x) <- sub(pattern="_", replacement=".", names(x),fixed=TRUE); x})
# Initialize our final data.frame
myAlleles <- unique(unlist(lapply(x, names)))
myAlleles <- sort(myAlleles)
myTable <- data.frame(matrix(nrow=length(myAlleles), ncol=length(x)))
rownames(myTable) <- myAlleles
colnames(myTable) <- names(x)

# Population the data.frame
for(i in 1:length(x)){
  myTable[ names(x[[i]]),i] <- x[[i]]
}

Hi John,

If you want a table of alleles x loci with the entries being allele frequencies, then private_alleles function would not necessarily be the way you want to go since it adds the population dimension to this.

If you set your population factor to NULL (e.g. pop(x) <- NULL), or only have one population, you can derive an allele frequency table using genind2genpop() followed by tab(freq = TRUE). After that, you can use tidyverse functionality to manipulate these data into a table (see below).

library("poppr")
library("tidyverse")
data("Pram")
# Selecting one population
JHC <- Pram[pop = "JHallCr_OR", drop = TRUE]
as.data.frame(t(tab(genind2genpop(JHC), freq = TRUE))) %>%
  rownames_to_column("loc") %>%
  rename(freq = JHallCr_OR) %>%
  separate(loc, c("locus", "allele"), sep = "[.]") %>%
  spread(key = locus, value = freq)

Can you clarify what you mean by "export calculated genetic distances"? Are you saying that you wish to export the initial distance matrix used to calculate the tree with the observed data, or do you want to export one matrix for each permutation of the data?

If you just want the initial distance matrix, you should use the distance function you want to use for the data. For example, if you were using a dissimilarity measure (e.g. diss.dist/prevosti.dist/bitwise.dist), you can export it as:

d <- prevosti.dist(myData)
write.csv(as.matrix(d), file = "/path/to/myDistance.csv", col.names = NA)

If, however, you want to do this the other way, then the task becomes a bit more difficult. You would have to define a function that will calculate your distance, write the matrix to a unique file (like above), and then return the original distance matrix.

Hope that helps,
Zhian

+1 for a tidy answer. Thanks Zhian! Those of us who are not as familiar with the tidyverse may find value in avoiding the use of the magritter pipe (%>%). This will allow us to examine the intermediate steps to get a better idea of what each individual function accomplishes. We can rewrite Zhian's example as follows.

library("poppr")
library("tidyverse")
data("Pram")
# Selecting one population
JHC <- Pram[pop = "JHallCr_OR", drop = TRUE]

JHC <- as.data.frame(t(tab(genind2genpop(JHC), freq = TRUE)))
JHC <- rownames_to_column(JHC, var = "loc")
JHC <- rename(JHC, freq = JHallCr_OR)
JHC <- separate(JHC, loc, c("locus", "allele"), sep = "[.]")
JHC <- spread(JHC, key = locus, value = freq)

Perhaps not as efficient as Zhian's example. But I found this helpful for learning the functions.
Thanks!
Brian
